verdict.reasoning: Patient states, "diarrhoea... it's lasting for like three days." and doctor restates, "you've had the diarrhoea for three days."
Patient says they have diarrhoea for three days and: "I can't go to work because I need to go... when I finish, I feel I need to go again... I need to be like close to the toilet uh, all the time."

Location: "the pain is mainly focus in, in the centre area of the abdomen, like under the belly, under the belly button." Relief: "it seems to be alleviate a bit, toilet" (after bowel movement). Tenderness: When asked about pressing tummy, patient says, "Ohh, it does a little bit."

Timing and food: Patient notes vomiting this morning after eating fruit (strawberries). Denial of blood: "I don't think there is blood because... it was the strawberries that I was having for breakfast... it wasn't blood." One clear recent episode is described; earlier they mention "I had a bit of vomiting," so stating one episode this morning is a simplification but consistent with the latest detailed account.
When asked about blood in stool: "An important question, have you noticed any blood?" Patient replies, "Uh, no, I haven't noticed any, any blood."

Fluids and intake: "maybe I'm not drinking enough water... I think I don't drink enough water." And, "I try not to eat a lot because... going to the toilet every ten minute." Also able to eat and drink some (e.g., fruit).

Chest pain: "have you noticed any chest pain?" Patient: ", no, I haven't , I haven't noticed any chest pain." Baseline asthma SOB: "I always have problems with my breathing, because of the asthma... apart of the normal, I haven't, I haven't." This indicates only baseline asthma-related dyspnea.
Patient reports: "I was sweating a little bit the last four days, but I... Not sure if, if I had bit of fever... I'm but I don't think so, I don't think. I don't know maybe."
Past medical history: "I have, I have, I have a, asthma, and I take some... inhaler."

Medication and brand change: "when I get a bit of anxiety, I, I use my inhaler... my inhaler kind of um, run out... I have uh, this brand, but I bought a new one here." Specific details of brand are not given, matching "details unknown."
Allergies: "I have an allergy. I have N, N, NK, NKDA allergy." This indicates no known drug allergies.
Family history: "my father. Because he died about um, ten years ago of bowel cancer."
Impact on work: "I can't go to work because I need to go... I need to be like close to the toilet uh, all the time." Also: "I'm spending some time at home."

Doctor’s assessment: "you might have eaten something bad, and it's causing your tummy pain... this is normally called gastroenteritis, so, an infection of the tummy." Symptoms in note (3 days diarrhoea, central pain relieved by going to toilet, nausea/vomiting, no blood, low intake and dehydration risk) all match patient’s history and advice to drink more due to losses.

Asthma status: Patient reports usual breathing problems from asthma but no new issues: "apart of the normal, I haven't, I haven't." Doctor adds inhaler is unlikely cause of tummy pain: "very unlikely for an inhaler to cause tummy pain, like this." This supports stable asthma with brand change and no acute exacerbation.

Anxiety and reassurance: Patient: "this is kind of uh... my, my worries" regarding father’s bowel cancer. Doctor: "most suggestive of an infection of your tummy and less likely to be something your father had." This reflects cancer-related anxiety and that current symptoms are less suggestive of malignancy.
Plan: "Number one is to drink lots of water and fluids, because you're losing lots at the moment." This is oral rehydration and increased fluids.
Plan: "please stay home for the time being until you get slightly better."
Plan: "Normally, things like antibiotics don't help, they make the situation worse." This implies avoiding antibiotics.
Plan: "make sure and look out for any fevers, so, if you start getting a temperature then you need..." and general context of monitoring for worsening symptoms during advice and safety-netting.
Safety net: "if you feel you're getting much worse, than I would suggest you go and see your GP in real, in real life, in person, so they can loot at your belly."

Doctor states inhaler is unlikely cause of GI symptoms: "very unlikely for an inhaler to cause tummy pain, like this." Discussion assumes continued use; no change or cessation is advised, consistent with "continue inhaler as usual."

Reassurance and future evaluation: Doctor: "the things that you've told me are most suggestive of an infection... less likely to be something your father had, but if your things don't get worse, then that's something that we can look up from the GP." This reassures and suggests future evaluation with GP if symptoms persist.
